summary: Defines managed objects for implementations of the Internet Protocol, independent of the IP version. It replaces RFCs 2011, 2465, and 2466 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the counters and tables a network manager reads over SNMP to see how a device's IP stack is working. One set of objects covers both IPv4 and IPv6, so a manager does not need a separate module for each.

subtitle: One set of SNMP objects for reading and controlling IP on a device, covering IPv4 and IPv6 together.

tldr.problem: IP was managed by three separate MIB modules: one for IPv4 and one each for IPv6 and IPv6 routers. A manager had to learn three sets of objects, and a device running both versions had to report the same facts twice.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4293 merges the three documents into one set of objects. Address types become an index, so a single statistics table holds rows for IPv4 and IPv6 side by side, and the address, prefix and translation tables carry an address type column too.
tldr.outcome: A manager can ask one device for both versions' traffic counters and addresses. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2011, RFC 2465 and RFC 2466 and is a Proposed Standard from April 2006 that has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 4293 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2006. It obsoletes RFC 2011, RFC 2465 and RFC 2466, and it has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: One MIB for Both IP Versions
sections.content:
One of the primary purposes of this revision of the IP MIB is to create a single set of objects to describe and manage IP modules in an IP version independent manner. Where RFC 2465 and RFC 2466 created a set of objects independent from RFC 2011, this document merges those three documents into a single unified set of objects. The ipSystemStatsTable and ipIfStatsTable are examples of updating objects to be independent of IP version: both contain counters to reflect IP traffic statistics that originated in much earlier MIBs, and both include an IP address type in order to separate the information based on IP version.

Another purpose of this document is to increase the manageability of a node running IPv6 by adding new objects. Some of these tables, such as ipDefaultRouterTable, may be useful on both IPv4 and IPv6 nodes, while others, such as ipv6RouterAdvertTable, are specific to a single protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Until now, IPv4 and IPv6 had their own MIB modules, so a device with both stacks reported the same kinds of facts twice under different names. This document merges them into one, with the address version as part of the index.

sections.title: What the Module Contains
sections.content:
The MIB does not provide native support for implementations of multiple stacks sharing the same address type. One option for supporting such designs is to assign each stack within an address type to a separate context, with the Entity MIB and the View-based Access Control Model Context Table providing methods for listing the supported contexts.

The MIB is composed of a small number of discrete objects and a series of tables meant to form the base for managing IPv4 and IPv6 entities. Some objects are meant to be included in all entities, while others are only conditionally mandatory. The unconditionally mandatory objects are mostly counters for IP and ICMP statistics. The conditionally mandatory objects fall into groups: objects for use in higher bandwidth situations, objects for use with IPv4, objects for use with IPv6, and objects for use on IPv6 routers. It is not expected that every entity will implement all of the objects in the MIB.

There are only a small number of knobs for controlling the general IP stack, and this MIB defines three general ones, only two of which are used for both IPv4 and IPv6. Objects are included for both protocols to enable or disable forwarding and to set limits on the lifetime of a packet, the TTL or hop count. The third knob, the timeout period for reassembling fragments, is only defined for IPv4, as IPv6 specifies this value directly. ipForwarding takes the values forwarding(1) and notForwarding(2), and ipDefaultTTL has the range 1 to 255.

A pair of tables conveys information about each protocol that is interface specific. Special note should be taken of the administrative status objects, which allow each protocol to be selectively enabled or disabled on an interface. With these objects and the ifAdminStatus object, an interface may be enabled or disabled completely, as well as connected to the IPv4 stack, the IPv6 stack or both. Setting ifAdminStatus to "down" should not affect the protocol specific status objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The module has a few global switches, such as whether the device forwards packets and what default lifetime it gives new packets, plus a set of tables that describe the counters, addresses, translations and routers of the device.

sections.title: The Statistics Tables
sections.content:
The IP statistics tables, ipSystemStatsTable and ipIfStatsTable, count the number of datagrams and octets a given entity has processed. Unlike the previous attempt, this document uses a single table for multiple address types; typically the only two types of interest are IPv4 and IPv6, but the table can support other types if necessary.

The first table conveys system-wide information, with counters for all interfaces rather than a specific set. Its index is a single sub-identifier representing the address type for which the statistics were counted. The second table conveys interface-specific information, with an index of two sub-identifiers: the address type, and the interface within that address type. The two tables have a similar set of objects intended to count the same things, except for the difference in granularity, and object ID ipSystemStatsEntry.2 is reserved so that the counters in the first table line up with their counterparts in the second.

Four objects describe the row rather than the system. The discontinuity objects, ipSystemStatsDiscontinuityTime and ipIfStatsDiscontinuityTime, let a manager tell whether an event has invalidated its understanding of the counters; a system being re-initialized or an interface being cycled are examples. The refresh objects, ipSystemsStatsRefreshRate and ipIfStatsRefreshRate, let a manager work out a sensible polling interval.

The RFC draws the general ordering of the packet counters. Received datagrams branch into header errors, multicast and broadcast packets, truncated packets, address errors and discards; datagrams that are forwarded go to InForwDatagrams and OutForwDatagrams, with InNoRoutes and reassembly counters on the way. Outgoing datagrams branch into OutNoRoutes, fragmentation counters, multicast and broadcast packets, discards, and finally OutTransmits. The discard counters may increment at any point in the processing path: packets discarded to the left of InNoRoutes cause the InDiscards counter to increment, while those discarded to the right are counted in the OutDiscards counters.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tables count packets: one for the whole device and one for each interface. Each row is marked with the IP version, so the IPv4 and IPv6 counts sit next to each other. A manager can also see when a counter was reset, so it knows not to trust a sudden drop.

sections.title: Addresses, Prefixes and Translation
sections.content:
The Internet Address Prefix Table provides information about the prefixes this entity is using, including their lifetimes. It gives a convenient place to which other tables that make use of prefixes, such as the ipAddressTable, may point, so the MIB can supply prefix information for all addresses while minimizing duplication and clarifying the relationship between addresses that share a prefix. This table is required for IPv6 entities.

The Internet Address Table lists the IP addresses, both IPv4 and IPv6, used by the entity, along with some basic information about how and when the address was formed and last updated. It lets a manager determine who a given entity thinks it is, and it is required for all IP entities.

The Internet Address Translation Table provides a mapping between IP layer addresses and physical addresses, as would be formed by the Address Resolution Protocol for IPv4 or by the neighbour discovery protocol for IPv6. The IPv6 Scope Zone Index Table specifies the zone index to interface mapping, so a manager can determine which groups of interfaces are within a particular zone for a given scope; the zone index information is only valid within a given entity, so indexes used on one entity may not be comparable to those on another. The Router Advertisement Table holds the non-routing information that an IPv6 router would use in constructing a router advertisement message; it does not hold prefix or other routing-specific information, which the router should acquire from the routing tables or from a routing table specific MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: Three tables describe what addresses the device has: which prefixes they belong to, the addresses themselves, and how each address maps to a hardware address. A fourth maps IPv6 zone indexes to interfaces.

sections.title: Default Routers and ICMP Counters
sections.content:
The Default Router Table lists the default routers known to the entity. It is intended as a simple list to display the information that end nodes may have been configured with or acquired through a simple system such as IPv6 router advertisements. Managers attempting to view more complicated routing information should examine the routing specific tables from other MIBs. The table is required for all entities.

The Router Advertisement Table is only required for IPv6 router entities.

There are two sets of statistics for ICMP. The first contains a simple set of counters to track the number of ICMP messages and errors processed by the entity. The second supplies more detail about the ICMP messages processed by the entity, with an index formed from two sub-identifiers: the first represents the address type, and the second the particular message type being counted. A row need not be instantiated unless a message of that type has been processed, so the row for a given message type may be instantiated before but must be instantiated after the first message with that type is received or transmitted, and after receiving or transmitting any succeeding messages of that type the relevant counter must be incremented. Both of these tables are required for all entities.
sections.plainLanguage: The module also lists the default routers a device knows about, and counts ICMP messages by type and by IP version, so a manager can see how much error traffic a link is carrying.

sections.title: Updating an Existing Implementation
sections.content:
Several general classes of change are required. The first and most major change is that most of the previous objects have different object IDs and additional indexes to support the possibility of different address types. The general counters for IP and ICMP are examples; they have been moved to the ipSystemStatsTable and icmpMsgStatsTable respectively. The second change is the extension of all address objects to allow for both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and the addition of an address type object to specify what address type is in use. The third change is the addition of several new objects to the replacement for a previously existing table such as ipNetToPhysical. The fourth change is the addition of completely new tables such as ipIfStatsTable and ipDefaultRouterTable.

For an implementation of the IPv4-only MIB, some general objects such as ipForwarding, ipDefaultTTL and ipReasmTimeout remain unchanged, and most of the rest of the general objects were counters that have been moved into the ipSystemStatsTable. The ipAddrTable has, loosely, been converted to the ipAddressTable, which is sufficiently different that writing new code may be easier than updating old code, and the ipNetToMediaTable has been moved to the ipNetToPhysicalTable. Two new tables, ipv4InterfaceTable and ipDefaultRouterTable, are required, as are several new ICMP counters.

For an implementation of the IPv6 MIB, ipv6Forwarding and ipv6DefaultHopLimit have been renamed and given new object identifiers within the ip branch but are otherwise unchanged; the new names are ipv6IpForwarding and ipv6IpDefaultHopLimit. The old ipv6IfTable was meant to replicate the ifTable, while the ipv6InterfaceTable is meant as an addition to it, so items duplicated between the two have been removed.
sections.plainLanguage: Existing software has work to do. Most counters keep the same meaning but move to a new table and gain an extra index, addresses gain a version column, and a few tables are renamed or replaced.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects defined in this MIB module have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

ipForwarding and ipv6IpForwarding allow a manager to enable or disable routing on the entity: disabling it could deny service to users, and enabling it could open a conduit into an area. ipDefaultTTL and ipv6IpDefaultHopLimit let an attacker decrease the diameter of the valid area so that packets are discarded before reaching their destinations. The interface enable status objects let an attacker enable or disable IPv4 and IPv6 on a specific interface. Modifying the ipAddressTable can cause a node to ignore messages destined to it, or to accept messages it would otherwise ignore. Modifying the ipv6RouterAdvertTable can interfere with the auto-configuration of all hosts on the link. Modifying ipNetToPhysicalPhysAddress and ipNetToPhysicalType could disable communication with a node or divert messages from one node to another.

Readable objects may also be sensitive. Essentially all of the objects in this MIB report on the status of the IP modules within a system, and the statistics tables supply information about the quantity and type of traffic the node is processing, which for transit providers may be considered sensitive. The address table provides a convenient list of all addresses in use by the node; each address in isolation is unremarkable, but the total list would allow an attacker to correlate otherwise unrelated traffic.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even if the network itself is secure there is no control over who on that network may GET or SET the objects in this MIB. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing to these objects can change how a device routes traffic, so an attacker who can reach them can cut traffic or expose a path. Reading them is also risky, because the address list and traffic counters help someone piece together who is talking to whom. The RFC asks for SNMPv3 with encryption and authentication.

items.title: Forwarding
items.text: Whether the device forwards packets for others: forwarding(1) or notForwarding(2).

items.title: Default TTL
items.text: The lifetime put in new packets, from 1 to 255.

items.title: Reassembly timeout
items.text: How long received fragments are held while awaiting reassembly; IPv4 only.
